props.title: They Shoot Horses, Don't They?
props.initialSlug: Dance marathon turns deadly in Depression drama

sections.content: They Shoot Horses, Don't They (1969)? stands as one of cinema's most brutal indictments of American capitalism and entertainment culture. Director Sydney Pollack transforms a Depression-era dance marathon into a microcosm of human exploitation, with Jane Fonda delivering a career-defining performance as Gloria, a bitter survivor whose dreams have curdled into cynicism. The film's relentless pacing mirrors the exhausting marathon itself, where desperate contestants dance for 1,200 hours straight while wealthy spectators bet on their collapse. Like Network (1976) and A Face in the Crowd (1957), it exposes how entertainment can become a weapon of mass distraction.

sections.content: The film's influence echoes through later works that examine entertainment as endurance test, from The Running Man (1987) to Battle Royale (2000) and The Hunger Games (2012). Its documentary-style shooting and use of actual extras from Depression-era Los Angeles creates an authenticity that makes the horror more immediate. The dance marathon sequences, with their mix of glamour and degradation, influenced later films like Nashville (1975) and Magnolia (1999) in their portrayal of entertainment as both salvation and poison. SUBHEAD: The Dance of Death

What sets They Shoot Horses, Don't They? apart is its unflinching look at the commodification of human suffering. The marathon's MC, played with sinister charm by Gig Young (who won an Oscar), represents the entertainment industry's predatory nature. His constant patter, promising glory while driving contestants to collapse, eerily presages reality TV competitions like Survivor (2000-present). The film's structure, building to an inevitable tragedy that's revealed in the opening flash-forward, creates a sense of doom that makes its social commentary even more powerful.
